\chapter{Juzgar}
\label{ch:es-juicio}
\hlchaptermodality{447}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can follow a clinic from the door to the results: which door when it is serious, what the doctor ordered, what somebody mentioned about it, and how to apologise for dropping the form.}

Read the message or notice this chapter's words exist for, then say the same thing back.

\section[el análisis]{el análisis — loosened apart}

\label{lesson:ES-C447-analisis}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{la sangre}, \textbf{el médico} and \textbf{el examen}. The doctor wants to know what is in your blood. Name what he orders.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el análisis}
\textbf{el análisis} — the analysis, and in a clinic \textbf{the test}.

\emph{Un análisis de sangre} — a blood test. \emph{Me han hecho unos análisis} — they have run some tests on me. \emph{Los resultados del análisis} — the test results.

This is the word on the form, and it is worth having before a waiting room rather than during one.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a noun that does not change}]
\textbf{el análisis} and \textbf{los análisis} are spelled identically. Only the article tells you how many.

Spanish does this to every noun ending in unstressed \textbf{-is}:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{one} & \textbf{more than one} \\
\midrule
el análisis & \textbf{los} análisis \\
la crisis & \textbf{las} crisis \\
el paréntesis & \textbf{los} paréntesis \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The reason is a rule you can use elsewhere: a word already ending in \textbf{s}, when its stress is \emph{not} on the last syllable, takes no plural ending. The same applies to \emph{el lunes} / \emph{los lunes} and \emph{el paraguas} / \emph{los paraguas}.

Contrast \textbf{el examen}, which does change — \emph{los exámenes} — and gains a written accent when it does, because the stress must stay where it was.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Greek \textbf{análysis}: \textbf{ana-} up, through, plus \textbf{lýein}, \textbf{to loosen}.

To analyse something is to \textbf{loosen it apart} — to undo the knots and see what the pieces are. That is a physical picture, and it is exactly what a blood test does to blood.

The same \emph{lýein} is in \textbf{paralysis}, a loosening of the body's control, and in \textbf{catalyst}, which loosens a reaction. Its opposite in Greek was \emph{synthesis}, a putting-together — which is what a Spanish lesson's last section is called.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el análisis}, then \emph{los análisis}
  \item the doctor has ordered a blood test
  \item what the two Greek pieces mean
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
A blood test? (\textbf{Un análisis de sangre}.) What is the plural? (\textbf{Los análisis} — unchanged.) What does \emph{lýein} mean? (\textbf{To loosen}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[comentar]{comentar — minding it over, together}

\label{lesson:ES-C447-comentar}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{pensar}. Say \textbf{el análisis}. Thinking is done alone. Name what you do when you think about something out loud, with somebody.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: comentar}
\textbf{comentar} — to comment on, and very often no more than \textbf{to mention}.

\emph{Me comentó que se jubila} — he mentioned to me that he is retiring. \emph{¿Lo comentamos mañana?} — shall we talk it over tomorrow? \emph{Sin comentarios} — no comment.

That middle sense is the one to take. In everyday Spanish \textbf{comentar} is much closer to \emph{mention} or \emph{talk over} than to the English \emph{comment}, which sounds like a verdict. A Spanish speaker \emph{comenta} things all day without passing judgement on any of them.

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{com-} together, plus \textbf{mens}, \textbf{mentem} — the \textbf{mind}.

To \emph{comentar} is \textbf{to mind something over with somebody}. The mind is sitting inside the word, and it is the same \emph{mentem} behind \textbf{la mente}, \textbf{mental}, and the ending \textbf{-mente} that turns a Spanish adjective into an adverb: \emph{rápidamente} is, at root, \emph{with a rapid mind}.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{the mind in it} \\
\midrule
comentar & to turn over together \\
la mente & the mind itself \\
rápida\textbf{mente} & with a rapid mind \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

That last row is worth keeping. Every Spanish adverb in \textbf{-mente} is a fossil of the word for mind, agreeing in the feminine because \emph{mens} was a feminine noun — which is why it is \emph{rápida}mente and never \emph{rápido}mente.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{comentar}
  \item he mentioned to me that the test results are back
  \item why every \textbf{-mente} adverb takes the feminine adjective
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To mention? (\textbf{Comentar}.) What is inside the word? (\emph{\textbf{Mentem}}, the mind.) Why \emph{rápidamente} and not \emph{rápidomente}? (\emph{\textbf{Mens}} \textbf{was feminine}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la urgencia]{la urgencia — something pressing on you}

\label{lesson:ES-C447-urgencia}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{la prisa} and \textbf{el hospital}. Say \textbf{comentar}. Being in a hurry is your own business. Name the kind of hurry a hospital has a door for.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la urgencia}
\textbf{la urgencia} — urgency, an emergency.

\textbf{Las urgencias}, in the plural, is \textbf{the emergency department}. The sign over the door of a Spanish hospital says \emph{URGENCIAS}, and \emph{ir a urgencias} is to go to A\&E.

The adjective is \textbf{urgente}: \emph{es urgente} — it is urgent. On an envelope or an email subject line, \emph{URGENTE} does the same work it does in English.

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{urgēre}, \textbf{to press, to push hard}. An urgency is something \textbf{pressing on you}, and English says the same thing when it calls a matter \emph{pressing}.

And you already have a second Latin word for pressing. \textbf{La prisa} is from \emph{premere}, also to press — the root of English \emph{press} itself.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{what presses} \\
\midrule
\textbf{la prisa} & \emph{premere} — you are pressed for time \\
\textbf{la urgencia} & \emph{urgēre} — the thing presses on you \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The difference is which way the pressure runs. \emph{Tengo prisa} puts it on you: \emph{I} am in a hurry. \emph{Es urgente} puts it on the matter: the thing itself is pushing. You can have \emph{prisa} about something that is not \emph{urgente} at all, and a genuinely \emph{urgente} matter can find you with no \emph{prisa} whatever.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
The ending is one you have met. \textbf{-encia} turns a verb into the state of doing it, the way \emph{experiencia} did in the chapter on paperwork.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{verb} & \textbf{the state} \\
\midrule
urgir & la urgencia \\
existir & la existencia \\
preferir & la preferencia \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So an unfamiliar noun in \textbf{-encia} will nearly always be hiding a verb, and the noun names \emph{the condition of that verb happening}. That is two endings now — \textbf{-ción} for the act and \textbf{-encia} for the state — and between them they cover a large share of the abstract nouns on any Spanish form.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la urgencia}, then \emph{urgente}
  \item we had to go to A\&E
  \item the difference between \emph{tengo prisa} and \emph{es urgente}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Urgency? (\textbf{La urgencia}.) The sign over the hospital door? (\textbf{URGENCIAS}.) What does \emph{urgēre} mean? (\textbf{To press}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[torpe]{torpe — from shameful to clumsy}

\label{lesson:ES-C447-torpe}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{feo}. Say \textbf{la urgencia}. \emph{Feo} judges how a thing looks. Name the word that judges how a person moves.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: torpe}
\textbf{torpe} — clumsy, awkward, and of a person's mind, slow.

\emph{Soy muy torpe con las manos} — I am very clumsy with my hands. \emph{Perdona, qué torpe} — sorry, how clumsy of me, which is what you say after knocking something over.

It does not change for gender: \emph{un niño torpe}, \emph{una niña torpe}. The noun is \textbf{la torpeza}, clumsiness — and also a blunder: \emph{fue una torpeza decir eso}.

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{turpis} meant \textbf{ugly, foul, shameful} — a heavy word, used of disgraceful conduct rather than of somebody who drops things.

Spanish kept the shape and moved the meaning from \textbf{how you look} to \textbf{how you act}, and softened it on the way. \emph{Turpis} was an accusation; \emph{torpe} is close to an apology.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the word} & \textbf{what it judges} \\
\midrule
\textbf{feo} & how a thing \textbf{looks} \\
\textbf{torpe} & how a person \textbf{manages} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Both are from Latin words for ugliness — \emph{feo} from \emph{foedus}, \emph{torpe} from \emph{turpis} — and only one of them is still about appearance. English took \emph{turpis} too, in \textbf{turpitude}, which kept the original severity and is now used almost nowhere.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
That softening is the useful part.

\textbf{Torpe} is not an insult in ordinary Spanish. It is what people call themselves after a small mistake, and calling yourself \emph{torpe} is a way of apologising without making the moment larger. Said of somebody else it is mild — closer to \emph{butterfingers} than to any real charge.

A word whose ancestor was severe and whose descendant is gentle is worth noticing, because the direction is not guaranteed. The reverse happens too. If you learn a word from its etymology alone you will pitch it wrong about half the time, so the root tells you where a word \textbf{came from} and never how hard it lands today.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{torpe}
  \item sorry, how clumsy of me
  \item what \emph{turpis} meant, and how hard \emph{torpe} lands now
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Clumsy? (\textbf{Torpe}.) What did \emph{turpis} mean? (\textbf{Ugly, shameful}.) Is \emph{torpe} an insult? (\textbf{No — it is nearly an apology}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(análisis, comentar, urgencia, torpe)]{(análisis, comentar, urgencia, torpe) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ES-R447-repaso-juicio}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say all four: \emph{the test}, \emph{to mention}, \emph{the emergency}, \emph{clumsy}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: what a root tells you, and what it does not}]
Three of these four are physical acts underneath, and knowing that helps.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{the act} \\
\midrule
\textbf{análisis} & loosening the knots apart \\
\textbf{urgencia} & something pressing on you \\
\textbf{torpe} & — see below \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Análisis} and \emph{urgencia} behave the way their roots suggest. \textbf{Torpe} does not. \emph{Turpis} meant \textbf{shameful}, a heavy accusation, and \emph{torpe} is now what you call yourself after knocking a glass over — nearly an apology.

That is the limit, and it is worth stating plainly: \textbf{a root tells you where a word came from and never how hard it lands today.} Meanings soften, and they harden too. Etymology is a hook for remembering and a guide to shape; it is not a guide to tone.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the doctor ordered a blood test
  \item he mentioned that it was urgent
  \item \emph{el análisis} and \emph{los análisis}, and what tells them apart
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\textbf{You can now follow a clinic from the door to the results} — which door to go to when it is serious, what the doctor has ordered, what somebody mentioned to you about it, and how to apologise for dropping the form.

Two endings close the set you have been collecting. \textbf{-encia} names the state of a verb happening, as \textbf{-ción} names the act. Between them they cover most of the abstract nouns on a Spanish form, and both have a verb inside worth looking for.

And one plural rule: a noun ending in unstressed \textbf{-is} does not change. \emph{El análisis}, \emph{los análisis}; \emph{la crisis}, \emph{las crisis}. Only the article moves.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The emergency department? (\textbf{Urgencias}.) A blood test? (\textbf{Un análisis de sangre}.) Clumsy? (\textbf{Torpe}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{(un mensaje desde urgencias) — read it, then do it yourself}

\label{lesson:ES-C447-sintesis-juicio}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{urgencias} and \emph{torpe}. One of them is where the writer is, and the other is how she explains getting there.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Read both, then answer.

\textbf{1 — de Lucía}

\begin{quote}
Estoy en \textbf{urgencias}, pero no es grave. Me caí bajando del autobús, soy una \textbf{torpe}. Me han hecho un \textbf{análisis} y una radiografía y estoy esperando.
\end{quote}

\textbf{2 — la respuesta}

\begin{quote}
¿Quieres que me acerque? Me \textbf{comentó} tu hermana que hoy librabas, así que no me pilla lejos. Dime algo cuando tengas los resultados.
\end{quote}

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item where Lucía is, and why
  \item what has been done to her so far
  \item what the second person offers, and how she knew
\end{itemize}

\begin{culture}
Two things in that exchange do more work than they look like.

\textbf{Pero no es grave}, in the first line, before any of the detail. A Spanish message from a hospital almost always leads with the reassurance, because the word \emph{urgencias} lands hard and the writer is defusing it immediately. Putting that clause last would read as burying it.

And \textbf{me comentó tu hermana}: not \emph{me dijo}, not \emph{me contó}. \emph{Comentar} is the mildest of the three — it says the sister mentioned it in passing, with no weight on it, which is exactly the right temperature for explaining how you happen to know somebody's day off. Choosing \emph{me dijo} would sound like she was told on purpose.

That is the difference between having the words and using them. Both writers pick the softest option available, twice each, and the message reads as calm because of it.
\end{culture}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Now your turn, out loud and then in writing. Four sentences from a waiting room: say where you are, say it is not serious, say what test they have done, and say somebody mentioned they might come.

Then check yourself: did you put the reassurance \textbf{before} the detail?
\end{tcolorbox}
